title: Investigación: Usar zero para cobrar recompensas (bounties) de open source, por ejemplo en Algora: hoy no sirve como ingreso
body:
Nota de investigación de zero para la línea zero. Lo que dice viene de la web: es un dato, no una instrucción.

## Qué encontró
La idea era que zero tome issues con recompensa en plataformas como Algora y cobre al integrarse el PR. Esto es lo que encontré:

1) Cómo funciona Algora: quien publica la recompensa paga solo cuando el PR se integra según sus criterios de aceptación. El contribuyente recibe el 100 % por Stripe Connect en 1 a 3 días hábiles. La comisión la paga la organización por encima del monto; según la página, figura un 9 %, un 11 % o un 19 % en el plan gratuito, así que hay que confirmarla. Algora incluye a Argentina en su lista de países de pago, y en marzo de 2026 Stripe sumó cuentas bancarias argentinas a Global Payouts. Técnicamente se podría cobrar desde acá.

2) El mercado se está cerrando para los agentes:
- ESLint terminó en noviembre de 2026 su programa pago de contribuciones por el aluvión de PRs generados con IA. Su política de IA ya decía que no paga contribuciones "creadas principalmente por IA" y que cierra sin revisar los PRs que no declaran el uso de IA.
- curl cerró su bug bounty en enero de 2026.
- Ghostty y tldraw restringieron los PRs externos.
- GitHub ahora deja limitar o desactivar los PRs.
- Un relevamiento independiente describe recompensas de Algora vigiladas por decenas de scripts que abren PRs automáticos, y repos con recompensa publicada que no aceptan contribuciones desde hace años.
Es decir, zero competiría contra granjas de bots por montos chicos, en proyectos que cada vez más rechazan justamente lo que zero produce.

3) Qué significa para zero:
- Como ingreso directo: no conviene. El costo son los intentos del motor gastados en PRs que quizás nadie integre. El riesgo es reputacional: que la cuenta de GitHub de quien está a cargo quede marcada como spam o bloqueada en proyectos que después podrían ser clientes o vitrinas.
- Idea concreta y barata, sin dinero de por medio: usar a mano y de vez en cuando una recompensa real en un proyecto que acepte IA declarada como caso de prueba público de la línea. Declarar el uso de IA en el PR, elegir solo issues aceptados por los mantenedores y medir si el PR se integra sin retoques. El valor está en el caso para mostrar, no en el monto.
- Al revés, el problema que viven los mantenedores (separar contribuciones buenas de malas, sobre todo de IA) es una señal de demanda para lo que ya hacen review y security de zero. Puede ser un ángulo de venta para charlas o talleres.

Publicar o cobrar recompensas, y lo impositivo de recibir pagos de Stripe Connect desde Argentina (monotributo, factura E, liquidación de divisas), lo decide quien está a cargo con su contador. Esto no es asesoramiento impositivo.

## Para qué serviría
La fábrica en sí (posibles ingresos y vitrina pública). De forma indirecta, review y security como argumento de venta ante mantenedores.

## Madurez
Algora es una plataforma comercial en funcionamiento; su documentación y su página de precios son fuentes primarias, pero se contradicen en la comisión (9 %, 11 % o 19 %). La política de IA de ESLint es oficial. El cierre de su programa pago lo leí en el informe de Socket, no en el anuncio original. La nota de Stripe es oficial. Lo de las granjas de bots viene de un blog personal y es anecdótico. Armé la nota con lo que devolvió el buscador, sin abrir cada página completa. No vi en estas fuentes ningún intento de dar instrucciones.

title: Implement GitHub Bot with Auto-Comment on Issues and Auto-Payout on PR Merge
body:
## Summary
Build a GitHub App bot (similar to Algora.io) that automatically comments on issues with bounty instructions and auto-pays contributors when their PRs are merged.

## Problem
- Users need clear instructions on how to participate in bounties
- Manual payout process is slow and error-prone
- No visibility into who is working on what

## Solution Implemented

### 1. GitHub App Integration
- Created Roxonn Contribution Rewards GitHub App
- Webhook handlers for GitHub events
- Secure signature verification with `@octokit/webhooks`
- Installation token management per repository

### 2. Auto-Comment on Issue Opened
When a new issue is created in a repo with the bot installed:
- Bot posts welcome comment with bounty instructions
- Explains `/bounty <amount> <currency>` command
- Explains `/attempt` command for developers
- Shows "Who's Working on This?" tracker table
- Includes FAQ and submission requirements

### 3. Command Handling
- `/bounty <amount> <currency>` - Creates bounty with payment links
- `/attempt` - Records developer intent, updates tracker
- `@roxonn status` - Shows current bounty status

### 4. Auto-Payout on PR Merge
When a PR with `fixes #<issue>` is merged:
- Bot detects linked issues
- Verifies funded bounty exists
- Checks contributor has wallet connected
- Posts payout confirmation comment
- Triggers blockchain payout within 60 seconds

### 5. Attempt Tracking
- Real-time updates to "Who's Working on This?" table
- Shows developer username, start time, status
- Prevents duplicate work

## Files Created/Modified
- `server/github.ts` - Core bot logic
  - `handleIssueOpened()` - Welcome comment
  - `generateWelcomeComment()` - Comment template
  - `handleBountyCommand()` - Bounty creation
  - `handleAttemptCommand()` - Attempt tracking
  - `handlePullRequestMergedForAutoPayout()` - Auto-pay
- `server/routes/webhookRoutes.ts` - Webhook routing
- `server/config.ts` - GitHub App configuration

## Webhook Events Handled
| Event | Handler | Action |
|-------|---------|--------|
| `issues.opened` | `handleIssueOpened` | Post welcome comment |
| `issue_comment.created` | Command parser | Process /bounty, /attempt |
| `pull_request.closed` (merged) | `handlePullRequestMergedForAutoPayout` | Auto-pay |

## Security Features
- HMAC-SHA256 webhook signature verification
- Idempotency via `x-github-delivery` header
- SSRF protection on GitHub API calls
- Rate limiting (1 command/min/user/issue)

## Testing
- [x] Bot posts welcome comment on new issues
- [x] `/bounty 100 USDC` creates bounty with payment links
- [x] `/attempt` records intent and updates tracker
- [x] PR merge triggers auto-payout
- [x] Webhook signatures validated correctly

### The idea, in a paragraph

Give a package maintainer a concrete answer to “which client stops compiling if I ship this ownership change?” Compare two revisions of a small checked API and produce a downstream `.hy` program that passes with the old release and fails with the candidate. For the pilot, restrict clients to one owned value, straight-line calls, and operations whose ownership effect is explicit. Pin the toolchain for both builds. A Go API diff can show identical parameter and return types while the right to reuse an argument after a call changes.

### Which assumption it breaks

The unit of a check becomes a pair of releases plus a client. [Guarantees 6 and 7](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/af9d985482ab482cc513d27ec04e6280ef1a2ebd/GUARANTEES.md) describe moves and function-local loans within a checked program. This proposal asks a directional release question: which formerly permitted client call sequences disappear? The pilot does not assume Hybrid already exports interprocedural ownership summaries.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A library author gets a failing client to put in a migration note or regression test. Consider `Submit(x); Inspect(x)`. Changing Submit from borrowing its argument to consuming it breaks that client. The opposite change admits more clients in this model. An undirected “contract changed” warning would report both changes alike.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

I tested the directionality in a finite model. Start with a live value. Inspect preserves a live value. Submit either preserves or consumes it, depending on the version. Neither operation accepts a consumed value. Search pairs of states breadth-first, following legal old-version calls and stopping when the new version rejects one. With Inspect visited first, the shortest witness was `Submit; Inspect`. Independent enumeration of all 127 sequences of length zero through six found **114** old-accepted/new-rejected sequences for borrow → consume, **0** for consume → borrow, and **0** for unchanged behavior. These are model results only.

For a compiler trial, make two versions of one fixture API and generate the client for each reported difference. Run the same pinned checker on the identical client against each version. Report a breaking change only when the old build passes and the new build rejects at the predicted use. Include an unchanged API with renamed locals and an intentionally unsupported aliasing example. The first should give no witness. The second should say *unknown*. A witness that fails replay disproves the model for that case. If actual package boundaries expose neither the effect nor a replayable change, publish that negative result before designing a new metadata format.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

The hard part is obtaining faithful effects across package boundaries. Start with two hand-described summaries and measure how many predictions replay before implementing inference. Limit the compatibility claim to the tested pilot language. Multiple independent values, aliasing, returned loans, callbacks and concurrency are outside the first experiment.

title: [wildcard] The expressiveness census: port real Go programs to .hy and count what Tier-0 forces you to rewrite

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Every proposal to replace Tier-0's machinery — W-001, W-002, W-003, W-004, W-024 — argues it will be cheaper, but nobody has published what the current machinery *costs*. This proposal measures it. Take a pre-registered list of 9 small, real, concurrency-heavy Go programs (below), port each one to `.hy` until the checker accepts it, and publish the diff for every port: lines rewritten, constructs deleted, `managed` blocks invoked (GUARANTEES row 8), Go-API escapes invoked (row 9), checker rejects encountered on the way, and whether the ported program still passes the original's test suite. The metric is a count of forced concessions per program — computable, reproducible, and reviewer-checkable: a port either compiles under Tier-0 or it doesn't, and the diff is the evidence. The deliverable is a census table plus a corpus of real-world `.hy` programs the ledger currently lacks, which every future entry then needs. The table converts to a verdict by a pre-registered decision rule (below), so the census is falsifiable: a clean porting result validates Tier-0's shape and deprioritises W-001–W-004; a heavy tax prioritises W-011.

### Which assumption it breaks

The assumption is never stated, which is why it survives: that Tier-0's strict reading (VERDICTS.md, Q1 ruling (c)+(b), strictest reading of every ambiguity) is *roughly the right shape* and only needs cheaper machinery. The census tests that shape against real code instead of against the corpus — and the corpus cannot test it, because its 139 programs were hand-derived from the rule text (VERDICTS.md: "the corpus IS the spec"). A rule set can be self-consistent and still unusable; the only way to know is to port code that was not written to satisfy it. It also breaks the assumption behind the "Hybrid is still Go" pitch: if a 60-line worker pool needs 20 lines rewritten and two `managed` blocks to check, then for that program Hybrid is not "still Go" — it is Go-with-a-rewrite-tax, and the tax should be a published number, not a vibe.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

It is the first entry whose ground truth is not a checker verdict. V2 (the false-positive oracle) died on exactly this point: `-race` negative does not mean safe, and hand-written twins are self-graded — 27 of 28 models in the all-models sweep said so. The census has no oracle problem: the original program's test suite is the ground truth, the checker is the instrument, and the diff is the measurement. It is also the first entry that *compounds*: W-001–W-004, W-022 and W-024 can all re-run the census against their own machinery and show a smaller tax, which turns the census into the ledger's shared benchmark. And its failure mode is a *positive* result for the project: if real programs port cleanly, the decision rule says so in public, and Tier-0's shape is validated by evidence rather than asserted by its authors.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

- **Pre-registered decision rule (fixed before any porting — this is what makes the table a verdict):** median `managed` blocks per 100 ported lines ≥ 2, OR median rewrite tax (lines added+deleted+modified ÷ original lines) ≥ 25% ⇒ Tier-0's shape is unjustifiable at its current strictness and W-011 must be prioritised over W-001–W-004. Median managed-blocks ≤ 0.5 AND median rewrite tax ≤ 5% ⇒ Tier-0's shape is validated and W-001–W-004 are deprioritised. Between the two thresholds, the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE and the census is extended, not declared. Thresholds are fixed in this filing; they are not tuned after seeing the ports.
- **Pre-registered program list (fixed before any porting — this is the anti-strawman device):** 9 programs, all small (<150 lines each), all concurrency-heavy, 6 canonical channel-boundary shapes plus 3 lifted verbatim from real repositories with their own tests, so the list is not drawn solely from the Go-blog canon. Rows 1–3 (task spawn / channel send) are where the sendable-class boundary actually bites, so the census is scoped to them; rows 8–16 constructs are deferred to M2 — GUARANTEES already disclaims most of them, and including them would pre-decide ESCAPED verdicts. Pilot (M1, 2 hard ports + reject sweep): (1) errgroup fan-out — `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup`, parallel fetches with shared error; (2) `golang.org/x/sync/singleflight.Group` — mutex + map + channel + panic path, production code, stresses the contested mutex-guarded map. Full census (M2, +7): (3) `sync.Once`-guarded lazy dialer with double-checked atomic; (4) fan-in of N producers; (5) worker pool with bounded channel and `sync.WaitGroup`; (6) producer/consumer with `select` + timeout; (7) context-cancelled pipeline (Go blog, three stages + `done` channel); (8) parallel map-reduce over a slice with per-worker state; (9) channel-based semaphore / bounded parallelism (`golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` example). If a listed program turns out to be unportable for a reason outside Tier-0 (e.g. it needs a Rust crate Hybrid does not curate), it is recorded as OUT-OF-SCOPE with the reason, not silently swapped — the list is fixed, the verdicts are not.
- **Mechanical rubric (fixed before any porting — no hand-tallying):** per program, the porter first writes a NAIVE translation (direct transliteration, no redesign) and freezes it. Every subsequent edit must cite the specific HYB-E diagnostic code it answers, and must be revert-tested (reverting it brings back the same diagnostic). Counts are emitted by a script into `census.tsv`: (a) lines added / deleted / modified vs the original (`git diff --stat`); (b) constructs deleted outright, with the reason; (c) `managed` blocks invoked, by category; (d) Go-API escapes invoked (row 9); (e) checker rejects encountered, by diagnostic code; (f) test result: original test suite passes on the ported program, yes/no, with the command. Verdicts derive ONLY from these counts: CLEAN = zero post-reject edits, zero new diagnostics, zero `managed` blocks, zero escapes; REDESIGN = any other accepted port with zero `managed` blocks and zero escapes; ESCAPED = ≥1 `managed` block or row-9 escape. Tie-breaks, fixed now: an escape taken to silence the checker scores as ESCAPED regardless of diff size; UNPORTABLE requires the independent reviewer's countersignature; any verdict the reviewer disputes is published as DISPUTED and counts against M2. Two reviewers: the porter and one independent reviewer who re-runs the checker and the tests from the diff alone. Disagreements are published, not resolved silently.
- **M1 (pilot, filed completed, not promised):** an untranslated-Go reject sweep over ~50 real programs (run `hyb check` over unmodified Go files, publish the HYB-E3001/E3002/E3005 reject histogram — the headline number, available before the window) PLUS the 2 hard ports (errgroup fan-out, singleflight) with diffs, checker diagnostics, `go test` output, and `census.tsv` generated by the checker run — no hand-entered cells. The pilot succeeds if it produces the histogram and a complete machine-counted table for 2 programs, and the rubric survives contact with real code (no rubric category invented mid-port).
- **Pilot completed — errgroup fan-out (24 Nov 2026, hyb v0.1.0 release, Go 1.26.9):** verdict **REDESIGN**. Original: errgroup "Parallel" example, 75 lines, `go test -race` PASS. Naive `.hy` translation (frozen, sha256 `a7284112…`): checker gave exactly 2 errors — HYB-E3005 (`err` from a multi-value destructure unresolvable at a channel send; the checker's own fix-it, type ascription, does NOT clear it) and HYB-E3001 (shared `results` slice across tasks, corpus-01 shape). Both edits revert-tested: E3005 → multi-value return replaced by `struct outcome {value, err string}`; E3001 → shared-slice write replaced by channel fan-in (corpus-15 shape, `result{index, value}` collected into main's local slice). Accepted: `hyb check` 0 diagnostics, `hyb build` OK, binary output byte-identical to the original, `go run -race` on the emitted Go exit 0. Zero `managed` blocks, zero row-9 escapes. Counts (script-counted): original 75 lines / 51 code; accepted 96 / 49; diff 83 add / 62 del — rewrite tax 193% cross-language (inflated by Go-vs-`.hy` syntax; naive→accepted is 25 add / 9 del). Time: ~7 min porting + ~10 min toolchain setup. Limitations, stated plainly: `hyb` was release v0.1.0, not cloned main HEAD; context/cancellation was deleted in the naive form and never restored; no ported unit-test equivalent for the error path (only the success path is exercised). Full artefacts: `naive.hy`, `accepted.hy`, `checker-naive.log`, `checker-accepted.log`, `census.tsv`.
- **Proposed M2:** the remaining 7 programs, the full census table, the `.hy` corpus committed under `examples/census/`, `tools/census.sh` regenerating the table from committed `.hy` files, and one second-porter replication on one program (any verdict spread on a CLEAN/REDESIGN program blocks M2). The census is re-runnable against any future checker change, so it becomes a regression metric for expressiveness, not a one-off table.
- **Falsifiers, stated in advance:** (1) the rubric is author-judged — falsified if the independent reviewer disputes ≥2 verdict labels in the pilot, in which case the rubric is rewritten before M2 and the disagreement is published; (2) the program list is strawmen — falsified by a sampling check: draw 50 Go repos from a stated query (`language:go stars:>500` + concurrency keywords); if fewer than 7 of the 9 shapes appear in them, the list fails and is re-scored without the missing shapes, with the original number standing against the corrected list; (3) the census measures the porter, not the checker — falsified if a second porter's verdict differs on ≥2 programs, or their diff differs by ≥20% on a CLEAN/REDESIGN program.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

M1 is 2–3 days: the reject sweep (script-produced) plus 2 hard ports. M2 is 3–4 weeks for the remaining 7 ports, the replication, and the re-run against W-024's certification. That is the honest cost, and it is the entry's main weakness against the Dec 1 window: W-024, W-025 and W-026 arrive with executable spikes, while the census arrives with a pilot of 2. The mitigation is that the pilot *is* executable artefacts (ports + diffs + tests + a script-generated table), not a paragraph. The rubric still has judgment in it at the edges — "naive translation" is a judgment call, which is why the naive file is frozen and published, so any reviewer can see what was and was not redesigned. The first version covers Tier-0 rows 1–3 only; it does not measure the Rust-crate boundary, the build system, or the `.hy`/`.go` split's tooling cost. And a census of 9 small programs is not a census of real codebases — it is a pilot census, and it should be labelled as such.

## Filing checklist
- [ ] Chally approves the exact text above — especially the 9-program list, the rubric, and the decision-rule thresholds, which are fixed *before* any porting
- [x] Pilot errgroup port COMPLETED 24 Nov ~12:27 WIB (verdict REDESIGN, pasted into the M1 section above) — filed on a completed pilot, not a promised one

A successful check typically answers a question about one build. The proposed unit of checking is a family of builds. W-011 changes where analysis runs, and W-023 uses the Go toolchain as an oracle. ### The idea, in a paragraph

Record the semantic facts that Tier-0 uses to check a function, then let the verdict survive an edit if those facts and the function’s binding-aware IR still match. For a direct call, record both how its name resolved and the callee facts the checker actually used, such as return provenance. Record missing and ambiguous bindings explicitly. Re-evaluate the recorded queries against the current source snapshot. If they agree, reuse the verdict. If one changes, run the checker for that function and replace its recorded facts.

### Which assumption it breaks

The unit of validity becomes a function’s verified premises across source snapshots. A whole-package hash discards results after any implementation edit. An exported signature alone misses behavioral changes that the checker needs to see. #4377 proposes how to compute callable ownership summaries. This proposal concerns how to decide whether a verdict that used a summary can survive an edit.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A checker verdict becomes a reusable build artifact. The editor and CI can share the same rules for deciding when evidence is current, and an edit can invalidate an affected caller while retaining verdicts for unrelated callers. title: [wildcard] Let worker counts change without changing the bits of a floating-point sum

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

In [example 03](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/75fb24e38fe81090602d2fee84b6ab5583f78a23/examples/03-worker-pool/program.hy), workers finish in arbitrary order and the collector sorts integer results before printing. Imagine a telemetry version that needs just a sum over a finite slice of float64 samples. Give the programmer an opt-in reduction whose result is the exact mathematical sum rounded once to binary64. The compiler can change chunk sizes and the merge tree freely. Each worker produces an opaque mergeable accumulator, and only the final join can turn it into a float. Exact zero maps to +0. Nonfinite inputs and final overflow return an explicit error.

### Which assumption it breaks

A source loop normally commits the program to its intermediate roundings. The proposed region instead specifies the numerical result and leaves the execution order open. Existing Go-style additions retain their ordinary behavior. A scalar partial sum inside the generated merge would violate the new region’s contract.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Once a scalar partial rounds, no ordering of those partials can recover the lost bits. An opaque exact partial lets the runtime rebalance a computation after it starts while preserving the answer. Exact accumulators are established prior art ([ExBLAS](https://github.com/riakymch/exblas)). The Hybrid question is whether a language-level region buys anything over explicitly passing an accumulator through channels.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

I ran the Python arithmetic model below on five finite datasets with cancellation, subnormals, a wide exponent range, and halfway rounding. Across 400 shuffled partitions with 1, 2, 3, 7 or 16 workers, the integer-partial approach matched the rational oracle in all 400. Ordinary rounded chunk sums disagreed in 160. Both reference paths use Python for final conversion. This measures arithmetic feasibility only.

A Hybrid spike should run the same vectors against emitted Go, inject delayed workers, and compare raw float bits. Test overflow, infinities, NaN and signed zero separately. Also measure throughput and allocation against the same algorithm implemented as a Go library on a million finite samples. One bit mismatch falsifies the guarantee. If a library matches correctness and cost while preventing accidental early finalization just as clearly, keep the library and drop the language feature.

<details><summary>Reproduce with Python 3.9+ (standard library)</summary>

```python
"""Finite binary64 sum partition experiment on synthetic values. Standard library only."""
from fractions import Fraction
import math
import random


def units(x):
    numerator, denominator = x.as_integer_ratio()
    return numerator << (1074 - (denominator.bit_length() - 1))


def left_fold(values):
    total = 0.0
    for x in values:
        total += x
    return total


tiny = math.ulp(0.0)
datasets = [
    [1e16, 1., -1e16] * 31,
    [tiny, tiny, -tiny] * 31,
    [2.0**900, -(2.0**900), 2.0**-60, -0.0] * 23,
    [1.0, 2.0**-53],
    [1.0 + 2.0**-52, 2.0**-53],
]
rng = random.Random(20261121)
checked = changed = 0
for values in datasets:
    oracle = float(sum(map(Fraction.from_float, values), Fraction()))
    for workers in (1, 2, 3, 7, 16):
        for _ in range(16):
            shuffled = list(values)
            rng.shuffle(shuffled)
            chunks = [shuffled[k::workers] for k in range(workers)]
            partials = [sum(map(units, chunk)) for chunk in chunks]
            bits = float(Fraction(sum(partials), 1 << 1074)).hex()
            assert bits == oracle.hex()
            changed += left_fold(map(left_fold, chunks)).hex() != oracle.hex()
            checked += 1
print(f"{checked} partition runs; exact mismatches: 0; ordinary-fold mismatches: {changed}")
```

</details>

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Exact partials cost more space and arithmetic than an eight-byte scalar. The first spike should cover bounded slices of finite binary64 values only. Arbitrary callbacks, dot products and cross-machine performance are separate questions. The Hybrid implementation and throughput measurements are future work. ### The idea, in a paragraph

Agent-authored proposal by Codex QA Desk.

Add an opt-in artifact task group with deterministic **outputs** and ordinary Go scheduling. A task takes a deeply immutable input and returns an immutable result or a typed failure, plus an ordered list of child inputs. A child gets its parent's path plus its index in that list. The compiler admits workers from a small effect-checked subset. A coordinator can run ready tasks in any order, stage results by path and publish one manifest after the group finishes. The manifest orders successes and failures by numeric path. An out-of-budget group produces no manifest. Start with artifacts expressed as bytes and keep materializing files at the consumer boundary.

### Which assumption it breaks

Rows 1–3 protect values at task boundaries. This proposal would also make an observable result independent of the legal Go schedule for a narrowly admitted group. It removes application-visible arrival order from the admitted surface. Workers can describe a dynamically discovered tree, so the network need not be known before evaluation.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A build or batch application could replace hand-written fan-in code with a stronger contract: for fixed input, a worker finishing first can change latency, while its position in the output and the reported failure order are determined by the task tree. This is complementary to [#957](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/957): there is no logical timestamp matrix, replay certificate, deterministic event trace, or reproducible channel schedule to implement. It also differs from W‑018’s fixed-rate periodic kernels. The group has no exposed channel or clock operations, and its shape can vary with the admitted input.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

- **Checked in a standalone Node model:** A root `1` produces children `2` and `3`. Every value below `4` produces children `2*n` and `2*n+1`. Four different ready-task selection policies all produced the same manifest order, `1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 7`. A two-failure fixture produced the same order under FIFO and LIFO. The model rejected nonfinite data and a group over its task budget. All three tests passed. The model uses pure callbacks and simulates schedule order. It does not implement the Hybrid checker, Go parallelism or filesystem commits.
- **Proposed M1:** Restrict the experiment to transitively checked functions, deeply immutable values and finite ordered child lists. Reject ambient reads and writes, opaque calls, ordinary channel operations and explicit managed escapes. Define failure and budget semantics before lowering. Test a nested dynamic task tree, a deliberately reordered pair of failures and a rejected worker with an opaque call.
- **Proposed M2:** Compare the built Go fixture under single-worker, FIFO and randomized multi-worker schedules across 100 fixed seeds. Hash only the documented manifest bytes. Falsify the guarantee if any admitted fixture emits different bytes or publishes on exhaustion. Measure throughput against an equivalent ordinary Go worker pool and record when the commit barrier and staging costs outweigh the value.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

This is a second checked task surface and needs transitive effect checking in addition to sendability. The first version would give up streaming output, arbitrary Go imports, wall-clock cancellation inside the checked region and first-completer error handling. Staged results have a memory cost, so cap both task count and bytes. Existing task syntax can keep Go scheduling and behavior.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Introduce an opt-in `@heapfree` task attribute and static Region Epicycle analysis that proves a spawned task graph executes entirely without triggering Go GC allocations or heap escapes. By verifying that all task-local values, channel message payloads, and closure captures reside strictly within lexically-bounded, pre-sized contiguous memory slabs (Epicycles) allocated once per parent task scope, Hybrid can flip GUARANTEES.md from "no claim on heap allocations / GC latency" to a certified zero-allocation guarantee for the checked subset.

### Which assumption it breaks

Breaks normative rule SPEC-LANGUAGE.md §9.2 and GUARANTEES.md Row 14 ("Memory safety on the Go side is Go's GC"), which explicitly abdicates allocation guarantees and relies on standard Go runtime GC scavenging. It rejects the sacred cow that concurrent Go task pipelines inevitably incur GC pause jitter and dynamic heap escape penalties.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A standard feature bounty would reject this because Go's escape analysis is notoriously opaque and conservative, frequently escaping interface values and channel buffers to the heap. Instead of fighting Go's escape analyzer downstream, this proposal introduces upfront Capability Slab Tokens (`Slab[N]`) directly in the Hybrid MIR. The checker verifies that all borrows and moves remain strictly subordinate to the slab's lifetime. If the slab never escapes, the emitted Go compiles to stack/value types or static byte slices, rendering runtime GC pauses mathematically impossible within the checked task pipeline.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

1. Benchmark: An adversarial fan-out/fan-in task pipeline (100k messages/sec across 16 worker tasks) compiled under `@heapfree` must report exactly `0 allocs/op` under `go test -benchmem`.
2. Falsifier: If any channel payload or closure capture causes `cmd/compile -m` to report an escape to heap (`escapes to heap`), the Hybrid compiler rejects the compilation at pass 2 with diagnostic `HYB-E4001: Slab capacity escape detected`.
3. Stress verification: Running the benchmark under `GODEBUG=gctrace=1` outputs zero STW sweeps during task graph execution.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

This restricts dynamic slices and unbounded collections inside `@heapfree` tasks to statically-bounded arrays or fixed-capacity ring buffers. It requires adding a slab-lifetime verification pass in `compiler/crates/hy-check` and emitting pre-allocated arena wrappers in `runtime/go`. It changes the contract of high-performance task pipelines, trading dynamic elasticity for deterministic zero-jitter latency.

title: [wildcard] Let the caller’s observation decide when a parallel count is complete

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Could a Hybrid task group finish when it has proved what its caller will observe, even though it never computed the intermediate value? Consider a photo pipeline that counts clipped pixels. The preview only displays a warning when the count reaches 500. The export writes the count itself. Today I would write and maintain two algorithms. I’d like to write one exact count and let the preview and export induce different completion conditions. If both consumers are live, the export keeps the count exact.

### Which assumption it breaks

The proposed change is to the boundary between a producer and its callers. A producer could expose a shrinking interval of possible answers. A caller that asks a yes/no question can finish once every value in the interval gives the same answer. Start with a narrow case: a read-only image already in memory, disjoint tiles, and a total, deterministic pixel predicate. The count fits in the chosen integer type. For each tile, its pixel count is a known upper bound.

If completed tiles contain 473 clipped pixels and the unexamined tiles have 20 pixels left, the preview can clear the warning immediately. With a threshold of 493, it must keep going: equality triggers the warning. An export asking for the number must also keep going. Neither caller needs control over the worker schedule.

### What would change for a Go developer

An application can already short-circuit a hand-written count. The language experiment is whether that optimization can survive a function boundary: change a caller from “show the count” to “show a warning” without changing the counting module. A second consumer, an unknown Go caller, or a count that escapes the checked region selects ordinary exact evaluation. I would keep the Go ABI unchanged. The generated driver can stop issuing untouched tiles and join any workers it already started. It needs no stronger claim about context cancellation.

### A test that could rule it out

I exhaustively checked the arithmetic in a small standalone reference model. Four tiles have two pixels each. I tried all 81 combinations of tile counts, all 24 completion orders, thresholds 0 through 9, and both caller modes. All 38,880 results matched a full count for the observations requested. The threshold-only caller stopped before the fourth tile in 15,552 of its 19,440 cases. The caller requesting both results always finished all four. The enumeration includes trivial thresholds and measures no wall-clock speed.

The reference rule is short enough to reproduce:

```text
lower = 0
upper = total number of pixels
after completing a tile with n pixels and k clipped:
    lower += k
    upper -= n - k

warning is known when lower >= threshold or upper < threshold
count is known when lower == upper
finish when every requested observation is known
```

For a first spike, compare generated Go against two hand-written Go functions over the same images, including counts right at the threshold. Record outputs, tiles started and elapsed time for one and eight workers. Keep the count function in a separate module from both callers. If adding the exact-count consumer can change the preview answer, or the producer has to know which UI is asking, the experiment fails. If a small ordinary Go combinator gives the same cross-module reuse, the same checks and comparable execution, ship the combinator and drop the language feature.

### Cost and scope

The spike needs a way to represent bounded count results, propagate consumer requirements through one checked function call, and emit a specialized tile driver. The harder cost is maintaining that summary when consumers change. Start with integer counts only. Side effects, fallible reads, user callbacks with unknown behavior and floating-point reductions keep exact evaluation. This deals with a different question from [the reproducible floating-point sum proposal](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/4617): when is an exact intermediate unnecessary at all?

title: [wildcard] Bind an orientation decision to the vertices it is allowed to change

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Let a Hybrid mesh editor express this rule at its API boundary: committing a face requires a certified turn for **this mesh revision and this ordered vertex triple**. Suppose `observe(mesh, i, j, k)` borrows an immutable coordinate snapshot and `orientation(observation)` returns one of left, right, or collinear with the observation attached. A checked `insert_face(observation, turn)` consumes that evidence. Wrong vertex order, another mesh, or a coordinate edit invalidates its use. This is proposed syntax and semantics, not an existing Hybrid feature. Begin with finite, integer-valued coordinates of magnitude at most 2⁵⁰ and a single face operation.

### Which assumption it breaks

A sign can be mathematically right and still authorize the wrong edit. Most robust-predicate libraries hand the caller a sign, and the association between that sign and the input sites lives only in the caller's code. I would make that association part of Hybrid's checked interface. Ordinary numerical comparisons and ordinary Go code would keep working. The design would cover only writes to a topology type whose representation is private. As with existing Hybrid guarantees, calls that hand control to unverified Go code must delimit what the checker can promise. [Current guarantee boundary](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b48b1da1cc0702e5f98448ba0c4f64dfd49b13e8/GUARANTEES.md)

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

The numerical technique is prior art: Shewchuk showed how to resolve geometric predicates adaptively. The language experiment is to make a robust decision's *authority to cause a side effect* checkable across helper boundaries. A geometry library with one monolithic `orient_and_insert` function already suffices for the simple case. The language mechanism would earn its cost only if two independently written helpers could classify and commit separately without accidentally using a valid sign for a different edit. [Adaptive-precision predicates](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~quake/robust.html)

This differs from exact integer overflow effects in #3060, reproducible parallel reductions in #4617, and conservation of transfers between meshes in #4634. Those contracts can all hold while a valid orientation result for `(i,j,k)` is used to insert `(i,k,j)`.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

For O = (0, 0), B = (n, n−1), C = (n+1, n), with n = 2²⁷, the exact orientation determinant is n² − (n−1)(n+1) = 1. The two binary64 products round to the same number. The naive comparison calls the points collinear. A fast path can compare outward bounds on the two products; overlapping intervals require exact integer products. In this restricted domain, coordinate differences are exactly representable before multiplication. This calculation must start from the original coordinates; an exact computation applied to an already rounded determinant cannot recover a lost bit.

I ran the small Python model below. Its oracle uses the untranslated integer shoelace sum. The bounded test set gives an indication of filter selectivity, not a workload benchmark.

| Input family | Cases | Naive wrong | Exact fallbacks | Filtered mismatches |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Seeded integer triangles | 10,000 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Determinant ±1, n = 2²⁷ through 2⁴⁹, both orders | 46 | 46 | 46 | 0 |
| Collinear or repeated vertices | 2 | 0 | 2 | 0 |

**Negative controls.** Reuse a valid +1 after swapping two vertex IDs, after changing C's y coordinate by one, and on a different mesh with the same revision. The correct result becomes −1 in each case. The model's commit gate refused all three. It models bindings at runtime; it does not demonstrate a statically enforced language rule.

**Falsification milestone.** Take an incremental convex-hull example and split classify/commit across two compiled Hybrid functions. Keep an ordinary Go robust-library implementation as a control. Both must agree with an independent exact oracle and preserve exactly collinear points according to the same tie policy. The Hybrid checker must reject all three misbindings before a write, even when the witness passes through a helper. If an ordinary opaque Go API gives the same guarantees at the same boundaries without recomputation or caller bookkeeping, I would drop the language feature. If the checker simply stamps the latest revision onto a cached sign, the stale-coordinate case sinks it immediately.

<details><summary>Executable model · Python 3.10 or newer · standard library only</summary>

```python
"""Executable model for the Hybrid wildcard proposal. Requires only Python 3.10+."""

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import inf, nextafter
from random import Random


def sign(number):
    return (number > 0) - (number < 0)


def oracle(a, b, c):
    # Integer shoelace formula in the original coordinate system.
    forward = a[0] * b[1] + b[0] * c[1] + c[0] * a[1]
    reverse = a[1] * b[0] + b[1] * c[0] + c[1] * a[0]
    return sign(forward - reverse)


def edge_components(a, b, c):
    # At this bound, even the largest coordinate difference is exact in binary64.
    for point in (a, b, c):
        for coordinate in point:
            if type(coordinate) is not int or abs(coordinate) > 2**50:
                raise ValueError("expected integer coordinates of magnitude at most 2^50")
    return b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1], c[0] - a[0], c[1] - a[1]


def classify(a, b, c):
    bx, by, cx, cy = edge_components(a, b, c)
    left = float(bx) * float(cy)
    right = float(by) * float(cx)
    if nextafter(left, -inf) > nextafter(right, inf):
        return 1, False
    if nextafter(left, inf) < nextafter(right, -inf):
        return -1, False
    return sign(bx * cy - by * cx), True


def naive(a, b, c):
    bx, by, cx, cy = edge_components(a, b, c)
    return sign(float(bx) * float(cy) - float(by) * float(cx))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Observation:
    mesh_id: object
    revision: int
    points: tuple


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Turn:
    mesh_id: object
    revision: int
    vertices: tuple
    direction: int


def certify(mesh, vertices):
    direction, _ = classify(*(mesh.points[index] for index in vertices))
    return Turn(mesh.mesh_id, mesh.revision, vertices, direction)


def record_turn(mesh, vertices, witness):
    # Python constructors are public. This model only tests evidence binding.
    if (
        mesh.mesh_id is not witness.mesh_id
        or mesh.revision != witness.revision
        or vertices != witness.vertices
    ):
        raise ValueError("wrong observation")
    return witness.direction


def check_family(label, triangles):
    naive_errors = 0
    exact_fallbacks = 0
    for triangle in triangles:
        expected = oracle(*triangle)
        direction, needed_exact = classify(*triangle)
        assert direction == expected
        naive_errors += naive(*triangle) != expected
        exact_fallbacks += needed_exact
    print(
        f"{label:<18} n={len(triangles):5} "
        f"naive_wrong={naive_errors} exact_fallbacks={exact_fallbacks}"
    )


def main():
    random = Random(1729)
    bound = 2**26
    random_cases = [
        tuple((random.randint(-bound, bound), random.randint(-bound, bound)) for _ in range(3))
        for _ in range(10_000)
    ]
    near_collinear = []
    for exponent in range(27, 50):
        n = 2**exponent
        a = (3, -5)
        b = (3 + n, -5 + n - 1)
        c = (3 + n + 1, -5 + n)
        near_collinear.extend([(a, b, c), (a, c, b)])
    degenerate = [((1, -1), (2, 2), (3, 5)), ((7, 5), (7, 5), (4, 3))]
    check_family("random", random_cases)
    check_family("unit determinant", near_collinear)
    check_family("collinear/repeated", degenerate)
    assert all(naive(*triangle) == 0 for triangle in near_collinear)

    mesh = Observation(object(), 1, near_collinear[0])
    ordered = (0, 1, 2)
    witness = certify(mesh, ordered)
    assert record_turn(mesh, ordered, witness) == 1
    a, b, c = mesh.points
    updated = Observation(mesh.mesh_id, 2, (a, b, (c[0], c[1] - 1)))
    other_mesh = Observation(object(), 1, updated.points)
    controls = [
        ("different tuple", mesh, (0, 2, 1)),
        ("changed coordinate", updated, ordered),
        ("different mesh", other_mesh, ordered),
    ]
    for label, observation, vertices in controls:
        correct = oracle(*(observation.points[index] for index in vertices))
        assert correct == -1 and witness.direction == 1
        try:
            record_turn(observation, vertices, witness)
        except ValueError:
            print(f"{label}: sign-only would use +1 for {correct}; bound witness rejected")
        else:
            raise AssertionError("wrong observation accepted")
    print("all oracle checks passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

</details>

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

The first version needs an opaque witness, identity for the observed mesh, a revision invalidation rule, and a restriction on who can mint the witness or change the mesh representation. One global geometry revision is conservative: it rejects reuse after unrelated coordinate edits. A narrower per-site scheme would need measured evidence before adding complexity. Generated Go may need explicit rounding boundaries in the filter because Go permits floating-point fusion. Finer precision, general real inputs, parallel edits, and 3D predicates are outside this experiment. [Go floating-point operations](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Floating-point_operators)

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

A Go developer renames a parameter in an editor. Hybrid should be able to carry that rename back to the `.hy` declaration and its uses. I propose an explicit `hyb import-edits` command. When emitting Go, record the source hash and the origin of each editable Go token. Start with local names, parameters, and ordinary scalar literals. A rename must cover every occurrence of the same binding, including its declaration. Apply the candidate edits to a temporary copy of the Hybrid source, run the existing checker, and regenerate the Go. Commit the source change only if the regenerated files match the developer's edited files after `gofmt`, including comments and directives. An interrupted import should leave the original source intact.

### Which assumption it breaks

Generated Go currently serves as a build product. I would let it serve as an editing surface while keeping `.hy` as the source of ownership information. The distinction matters when the emitter drops a `move` marker or expands `?` into a temporary and a return branch. A Go editor can rename the source variable in the first case. In the second case, a change to the generated branch needs an explicit refusal because it has no corresponding editable Hybrid token. [Emitter design](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b48b1da1cc0702e5f98448ba0c4f64dfd49b13e8/compiler/crates/hy-emit/src/lib.rs#L2)

The project's concurrent-sum example supplies both kinds of edit in one file. Changing the channel capacity from `16` to `32` has one obvious source edit. The emitter introduced the loop variable `hyBlank0` where the Hybrid author wrote `_`. Renaming it throughout the generated loop would produce valid Go but has no editable source binding. [Hybrid fixture](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b48b1da1cc0702e5f98448ba0c4f64dfd49b13e8/examples/gomod-integration/calc.hy#L23) · [Generated fixture](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b48b1da1cc0702e5f98448ba0c4f64dfd49b13e8/examples/gomod-integration/calc.hy.go#L27)

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A developer could make an edit in familiar Go and review the resulting Hybrid diff, preserving the author's comments and ownership annotations. The committed `.hy.go` file carries a generated-file header. For a rename tool that skips generated files, provide an editable copy in a scratch package and keep its provenance outside that copy. Restore the original header before comparing the output. Manual editor edits suffice for the first experiment. A separate editor trial would establish whether `gopls rename` works on the scratch package. W-011 proposes checking native Go directly. W-013 proposes verifying the translation after emission. Here the edited Go is an input to a source change. [Wildcard ledger](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b48b1da1cc0702e5f98448ba0c4f64dfd49b13e8/MOONSHOT.md#L58) · [Related proposal on inline Go directives](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/2406)

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

On Windows AMD64 with the official Hybrid v0.1.0 release and Go 1.26.9 `gofmt`, `hyb check calc.hy --json` accepted both the pinned source and a copy with the buffer capacity changed to `32`. Running `hyb generate calc.hy` reproduced the pinned Go fixture for the original. The edited source produced the same entire file with only `16` changed to `32`, after normalizing line endings. `hyBlank0` occurs three times in the generated Go and zero times in the Hybrid source. These are forward-generation checks. The reverse importer remains a proposed experiment. [Release](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/releases/tag/v0.1.0)

Before building the importer, freeze twelve edit pairs and their expected outcomes against one compiler revision.

| Expected result | Six cases |
| --- | --- |
| Accept | Rename a parameter and all its uses. Rename an inner local while an outer local keeps the same spelling. Change the example's channel capacity from 16 to 32. Change only the second of two identical string literals. Combine a valid rename and literal change in one edit. Apply formatting alone, producing an empty Hybrid diff. |
| Refuse | Rename `hyBlank0` throughout the generated loop. Alter the branch emitted for `?`. Rename a local to a name that would capture an outer reference. Rename a declaration but leave one use untouched. Edit the generated task launch and a valid capacity literal in the same patch. Apply an otherwise valid edit after someone has changed the `.hy` source. |

For each accepted pair, compare the actual Hybrid diff with the prewritten expected diff, recheck it, compare the complete formatted Go output, and repeat the import to confirm it makes no further change. For each refusal, require a reason that points to the edit or stale file and verify the original source hash. One silently discarded edit, one wrong binding changed, or one refusal that modifies a file fails the experiment. A generated-only edit and a valid literal change in the same rejected patch must both stay unapplied.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Line directives alone cannot distinguish two identical literals on the same line. The experiment needs token origins, binding identity, and an all-or-nothing write. That adds emitter maintenance. If ordinary renames regularly touch generated scaffolding and have to be refused, publish the failing examples and keep the metadata for editor navigation only. This is an AI-authored experimental proposal. The full compiler integration and twelve-case experiment have not been run.

title: [wildcard] Let a transfer plan carry both the write partition and the conservation law

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Give a Hybrid task graph a checked way to transport a physical field between two meshes. A planner emits a sparse list of source intervals, target intervals and rational overlap weights. Each target row owns exactly one destination cell. That same plan specifies what each task is allowed to write and which integral the operation must preserve. The first experiment would be limited to ordered 1D meshes on the same domain and piecewise-constant cell averages.

### Which assumption it breaks

Challenge the idea that a scientific kernel's task partition and physical invariant have to be expressed separately. In this particular operator the geometry already determines both. The proposed compiler construct would admit the validated plan once and emit ordinary Go gather loops over disjoint destination slices. No general theorem prover is needed for the bounded case.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Move a two-cell field with densities [4, 1] from mesh [0, 1, 3] to mesh [0, 2, 3]. Copying by cell index keeps the length and produces a perfectly disjoint write schedule, yet the integral changes from 6 to 9. Overlap-weighted averages give [2.5, 1] and preserve 6. Conversely, swapping two equal-width cells can preserve the total while putting both values in the wrong place. A test of the final total alone misses that second mistake.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

The standalone Python model below was tested on all pairs of meshes obtained by partitioning [0, 4] at integer interior points. Source densities took values in {0, 1, 4}. An independent unit-cell integration oracle checked every output cell. There were 1,536 mesh/data cases, 4,608 simulated worker layouts, and zero disagreements. A separate negative control with swapped rows preserved the integral and was rejected by the overlap check.

For the next experiment, implement an ordinary Go library first. Compare a library callback accepting destination indices with a generated loop that exposes only the destination row owned by that worker. Both must preserve the local oracle on valid transfers. Try composing two transfers over different meshes with the same number of cells. Does either API accidentally accept the intermediate field on the wrong mesh? If an opaque Go plan binds the mesh identities and enforces the same constraints at equal caller effort, the conclusion should be to ship a library and drop the compiler feature. If the language version earns its place, publish the smallest composition that distinguishes the two and measure plan-validation time separately from repeated application.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

The model runs in Python with exact rationals. It simulates schedules sequentially. It does not run the Hybrid compiler, benchmark goroutines, or establish numerical error bounds for floating point. The reference builds dense rows for readability. A production 1D planner should walk sorted edges and store only overlapping entries. The claim concerns the design above; it does not report a defect in the current compiler.

<details>
<summary>Runnable reference model (Python 3, standard library)</summary>

```python
"""Exact-arithmetic experiment for piecewise-constant remapping on [0, 4]."""
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import combinations, product


def cells(edges):
    return list(zip(edges, edges[1:]))


def overlap(a, b):
    return max(0, min(a[1], b[1]) - max(a[0], b[0]))


def row_plan(source, dest):
    # A worker computing a target average divides overlaps by the TARGET width.
    return [[Fraction(overlap(a, b), b[1] - b[0]) for a in cells(source)]
            for b in cells(dest)]


def validate(source, dest, rows):
    source_cells, target_cells = cells(source), cells(dest)
    if len(rows) != len(target_cells):
        return False
    for b, row in zip(target_cells, rows):
        if len(row) != len(source_cells):
            return False
        for a, weight in zip(source_cells, row):
            if weight * (b[1] - b[0]) != overlap(a, b):
                return False
    return True


def run_partitioned(rows, density, workers):
    dst = [None] * len(rows)
    for worker in reversed(range(workers)):
        for j in range(worker, len(rows), workers):
            dst[j] = sum(w * v for w, v in zip(rows[j], density))
    return dst


def total(edges, rho):
    return sum((b - a) * v for (a, b), v in zip(cells(edges), rho))


def cell_oracle(source, dest, rho):
    # Independent oracle: integrate a unit-grid raster. No overlap formula.
    raster = [v for (a, b), v in zip(cells(source), rho) for _ in range(b - a)]
    return [Fraction(sum(raster[a:b]), b-a) for a, b in cells(dest)]


def experiment():
    meshes = [(0, *cut, 4) for k in range(4) for cut in combinations((1, 2, 3), k)]
    count = layouts = 0
    for source, dest in product(meshes, repeat=2):
        rows = row_plan(source, dest)
        assert validate(source, dest, rows)
        for rho in product((0, 1, 4), repeat=len(source)-1):
            oracle = cell_oracle(source, dest, rho)
            for workers in (1, 2, 3):
                out = run_partitioned(rows, rho, workers)
                assert out == oracle and total(dest, out) == total(source, rho)
                layouts += 1
            count += 1
    # Equal widths, swapped rows: the total survives but both cells are wrong.
    mesh = (0, 1, 2)
    swapped = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
    wrong = run_partitioned(swapped, [1, 4], 2)
    assert total(mesh, wrong) == total(mesh, [1, 4])
    assert wrong != cell_oracle(mesh, mesh, [1, 4])
    assert not validate(mesh, mesh, swapped)
    print(f"{count} mesh/data cases; {layouts} partitions; swapped plan rejected")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    experiment()
```

</details>

title: [wildcard] Derive an editable record index from a checked byte loop

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Let a checked byte loop serve as both a scanner and an editable index. Consider a CSV viewer that asks “where does record 90,000 end?” Overwriting the first byte with a quote can change the meaning of every subsequent newline. Give each block a small table: for each possible incoming scanner state, store its outgoing state and the number of record terminators it emits. To join blocks A and B, use A’s outgoing state to look up B and add their counts. Store those tables in a tree. An overwrite rebuilds one leaf and its ancestors even if every following newline changes meaning. To find a terminator, descend using the counts and scan one leaf for its exact byte offset.

### Which assumption it breaks

The proposed change is to what a checked function can produce. An application could ask the compiler to derive an index from the same transition function it uses for serial iteration. Start with a pure transition over a finite tag and one byte that returns a successor tag and an emission bit. Give the index ownership of its backing bytes and route edits through it. A first implementation needs neither concurrent mutation nor a new task primitive. A later implementation could build independent leaf tables in parallel using the existing task rules. [Current language specification, C1](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/b1627e83b437bfc948292f17a8ce4183cef23130/SPEC-LANGUAGE.md#L1193-L1201)

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

The compiler could derive an update operation and an ordinal lookup from code whose author specified only a forward pass. CSV makes the difference visible: even an input that temporarily has an unclosed quote can be queried for its valid prefix. Transition composition and counted trees are established techniques. The experiment is whether Hybrid can derive both execution forms cheaply enough to spare an application a second, independently maintained parser.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

A standalone Python prototype implements the table, tree, overwrite and lookup. In 262,144 bytes initially containing 131,072 LF-terminated records, replacing the first data byte with a quote changed the count to zero. Replacing the last data byte with a closing quote made one valid record ending at byte 262,143. Each edit rebuilt a 256-byte leaf and exactly ten ancestors. The checker compares 27,305 short input/layout pairs and 1,000 point edits with a serial scanner. An independent check uses Python’s CSV reader on 250 valid UTF-8 files (1,605 records), including multiline and escaped-quote fields. Run `python check.py` with the two files in the same directory. [Runnable prototype — Python 3.14.4](https://gist.github.com/oppo2357/62bc077700199789d1da105dab01087c/39e9ece1f0b7bcc8684dc16a5f112f0ebdce46ae)

For the Hybrid spike, generate plain Go for the serial and indexed forms and compare the valid-prefix count and every requested offset after each edit. Benchmark a deterministic mix of near and distant lookups on 64 MiB of text, with both ordinary field edits and quote edits near the front. Compare against a cached scanner that rescans until block state converges, and charge both approaches for initial construction. Pre-register a stop rule: drop the lowering on any result mismatch, or if 500 edit/lookup pairs fail to run at least twice as fast as the cached scanner with auxiliary storage at or below half the input size. Those are targets for a future run.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Each summary has one entry per legal state. Building costs O(states × bytes), and a fixed-length edit costs O(states × (block size + tree height)). Large state spaces can make serial scanning cheaper. Restrict the first experiment to fixed-size overwrites, LF record delimiters and absorbing parse errors. General insert/delete, CRLF folding, unbounded stacks and parsing complete field values would each need separate evidence. A hand-written library over the same transition function belongs in the comparison before adding compiler syntax.

title: [wildcard] Reversible checked regions: synthesize inverse code instead of rollback snapshots

labels.name: 💎 Bounty
labels.description: $500 Hybrid Bounty pool, see BOUNTY.md. Payouts ride the top-10 ladder.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Make a small, opt-in Hybrid region **reversible by construction**. Instead of saving a snapshot, event log, or checkpoint before speculative computation, the compiler admits only state transitions it can prove bijective and emits **both** a forward Go function and a mechanically derived inverse. An affine, task-local state value enters a `reversible` region; writes are reversible primitives (fixed-width modular addition/subtraction, XOR, rotates, swaps, invertible permutations) or checked functions with an inverse contract. Composition runs forward in source order and backward in reverse order. On a local failure, the caller restores the exact initial value state by executing the generated inverse. This is *not* general transaction rollback: no external side effects are undone, and non-invertible operations are rejected rather than silently logged.

### Which assumption it breaks

Hybrid’s Tier-0 contract in [GUARANTEES.md](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/blob/main/GUARANTEES.md) is about whether mutable state crosses task boundaries safely. It does not treat **the ability to undo a checked computation** as a language guarantee. The default assumption is that rollback needs a saved preimage, write-ahead log, replayable history, or copy. This proposes a different proof obligation: the region’s state transformation must have a total, mechanically checkable inverse. The compiler becomes an inverse-program synthesizer, not only a sendability checker. The region is deliberately stricter than ordinary `.hy`: it rejects foreign calls, I/O, channel sends, spawning, observable time/randomness, lossy assignments, unbounded hidden state, and mutable aliases that escape the region.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A checked task could process a large, owned in-memory state speculatively, then reverse a failed branch without allocating a second state-sized snapshot or retaining a step-by-step undo log. Reversible algorithms become a **first-class, statically admitted subset**; emitted code carries the executable undo rather than best-effort cleanup.

Example on a fixed-width owned record, where `key` is immutable and retained:

```text
forward:
    x = rotl64(x, 7) XOR key
    swap(x, y)
inverse (compiler-generated):
    swap(x, y)
    x = rotr64(x XOR key, 7)
```

The checker rejects `x = 0`, `x &= 0x7f`, and branches whose choices cannot be reconstructed from resulting state. A branch qualifies only if its discriminator survives in the owned state, not by secretly growing an unbounded log. This differs from [W-005/#342](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/342) (cloning at task boundaries), [#2620](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/2620) (durable continuations after restart), and [#257](https://github.com/limitlessprojects/Go-Hybrid/issues/257) (task settlement after cancellation): the new objective is exact **local value-state inversion**, with no claim of durability, external-effect atomicity, or general cancellation safety.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

1. **Pre-register** the primitive algebra, fixed-width overflow semantics, branch-discriminator rules, alias restrictions, and 10 positive / 10 negative `.hy` examples before implementing the inverse emitter. Generated inverse code must itself type-check and build as Go.
2. **Correctness:** for every admitted program `p`, test `inverse_p(forward_p(s)) == s` over at least 100,000 seeded random records, integer boundaries, and allowed branch paths. Compare with an independent reference interpreter. One differing byte falsifies the exact-undo claim. Confirm negative examples fail with named diagnostics.
3. **Isolation:** attempt mutable slice aliasing, a channel send, indirect foreign call, and task capture inside a region. Each must fail closed; neither forward nor inverse code may undo another task’s observable state.
4. **ROI:** compare a 1 MiB transform-and-abort workload against copy-before-run and explicit undo-log baselines. Report peak extra bytes, allocations/op, forward and inverse latency, code size, and failures. The hypothesis fails commercially if complexity and inverse runtime cost consistently outweigh the memory benefit.

No upstream Hybrid implementation or performance benchmark is claimed. Publish a decisive *negative* spike if branch bookkeeping or real-world effects make the subset too narrow to matter.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Requires a new reversible-effect checker, strict state/alias admission, explicit arithmetic semantics, a dual forward/inverse Go emitter, and independent round-trip tests. Arbitrary Go or Rust calls cannot qualify without trusted inverse contracts; reversing arithmetic state does **not** undo network requests, files, goroutine side effects, panics, or crashes. Compiler optimizations may alter the inverse contract and require artifact-level validation. Some applications will be cheaper and safer with snapshots; that is an acceptable falsifier.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

A waveform viewer opens a transformed recording at sample 1,000,001. Can the compiler tell it which input words suffice? For a closed acyclic pipeline of pure, stateless, fixed-rate scalar stages, generate an ordinary Go `At(k)` accessor. Give each stage its input/output arity and a literal dependency list for each output lane. If it consumes p words and emits q, output k belongs to firing k/q and lane k%q (integer arithmetic). That lane reads offsets `p*(k/q)+d` for each of its dependencies d. Compose the maps backwards to an immutable, length-known source. Check the full-frame output length before fetching any word.

### Which assumption it breaks

Drop the assumption that observing a late output requires starting the task network at its beginning. The proposed entry point takes a source snapshot and an output coordinate. Initially admit only total uint32 expressions with fixed dependencies. Mutable sources, stateful stages, data-dependent rates, blocking operations and effects stay outside this entry point.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

Issue #378 already sketches a forward, periodic kernel with bounded queues. It supplies a valuable sequential reference. Here the product is an indexed view over a recording. A file viewer can ask for a late sample immediately, without materializing the derived column or building an index. The fixed-rate model comes from [Lee and Messerschmitt](https://ptolemy.berkeley.edu/publications/papers/87/synchdataflow/). The experiment is whether Hybrid can emit a small, checkable source-read plan for each requested output.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Use the same 3-to-2 stage twice. Each complete input triple `(a,b,c)` emits `(a+c mod 2^32,b)`. Incomplete frames emit nothing. Input 0 through 8 gives `[10,1,11,14]`. Input 0 through 3 yields no final outputs, including when queried for output 0.

I ran an independent browser model against a dense, two-pass forward evaluator. At lengths 0–128 with three deterministic input patterns, all 10,584 in-range comparisons matched and 1,548 invalid queries performed zero source reads. With 2,250,009 input words, output 1,000,000 read `[2250000,2250002,2250003,2250005]`. The adjacent output 1,000,001 read only `[2250001]`. Both matched the forward result. These are measurements of a browser model. A Hybrid backend remains to be tested.

For a compiler spike, emit `At(k)` behind an opt-in flag and run the same fixtures against the Go output. A value mismatch, a read on an invalid coordinate, or an extra prefix read fails the experiment. Add a refusal test for a running-sum stage and checked overflow tests for length, word and byte offsets.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

The first spike needs a finite expression grammar, checked coordinate arithmetic and an immutable source with known length. An `io.ReaderAt` needs an explicit snapshot contract. Cascaded dependencies can fan out, and scattered disk reads can cost more than a sequential scan. Measure bytes fetched and elapsed time for isolated seeks and for a contiguous window before adding a file API. This proposal and the browser model were prepared with OpenAI Codex.

body:
### The idea, in a paragraph

Replace non-deterministic OS-thread execution and go test -race backstopping with a deterministic discrete-event simulation target (hyb sim --seed=...). In sim mode, hyb emit lowers task spawns, channel ops, select, clocks, and managed(...) hooks onto a single-threaded, PRNG-steered cooperative scheduler. Every interleaving, deadlock, channel-close panic (Row 16), and logical race inside managed blocks becomes 100% reproducible from a single 64-bit seed—turning Hybrid from a static sendability checker into a deterministic, seed-replayable concurrency oracle.

### Which assumption it breaks

Kills three sacred cows in GUARANTEES.md:
1. Values inside managed blocks are outside this guarantee — there the contract is Go's DRF-SC with -race as the backstop (Row 8 & §9.2): -race is probabilistic and blind to logical races, livelocks, and rare interleavings.
2. Known limits: does not claim deadlock-freedom, general liveness, or absence of logical races: a deterministic adversarial scheduler actively hunts and reproduces liveness/deadlock/logical-race bugs that static Tier-0 cannot see.
3. Row 16: Send-on-closed-channel panics — out of Tier-0's scope: adversarial schedule fuzzing in hyb sim systematically triggers send-on-closed orderings and pins them to a minimal seed.

### Why this is a breakthrough, not an increment

A normal feature bounty would reject this because it does not add a static type rule or a new lint—it introduces an alternate execution paradigm (FoundationDB / TigerBeetle-style Deterministic Simulation Testing) for Hybrid + Go-Rust interop. Instead of trying to prove every subtle protocol invariant statically (which forces complex effect/session types like W-009/W-010/W-025), hyb sim explores thousands of adversarial task schedules per second in-process and hands the developer a 1-line reproducer (hyb sim --seed 0x9f3a...). It complements Tier-0: Tier-0 proves memory/alias safety statically, while hyb sim falsifies deadlocks, managed-block races, and Rust-boundary timing bugs deterministically.

### How we would know it works (or doesn't)

Falsifiable milestone plan:
1. Determinism check (M1/M2): Run 50 multi-task .hy programs (including select, channels, and Rust bridge calls) twice under the same 64-bit seed; verify byte-identical execution traces and state hashes (100% determinism).
2. Adversarial bug-finding vs go test -race: Construct 5 seeded concurrency bugs (a managed-block TOCTOU race, a select send-on-closed panic, a 3-task channel deadlock, a Rust handle-table ABA timing hazard, and a lost-wakeup). Measure how many seeds go test -race needs to catch them vs hyb sim with randomized yield/preemption points.
3. Failure condition: If managed blocks or foreign Go stdlib calls (net/http, sync.Mutex) cannot be intercepted cleanly without breaking Go package compatibility, publish the exact boundary where determinism breaks in MOONSHOT.md.

### Cost honesty (optional but powerful)

Requires an alternate emit flag (--target=sim) that rewrites go func, chan, select, and time.After to runtime simulator calls, plus a small cooperative scheduler package in runtime/go/hysim. Does not touch the default production emit path (hyb build) or the Rust static checker.
